summaries.example: Think about a box of crayons. “Color” is a broad property, so it is a determinable. “Red” is a more exact color, so it is a determinate of color. “Scarlet” can be an even more exact determinate of red. A crayon can be red without being scarlet, but something scarlet must also be red and colored.
summaries.summary: This entry explains the difference between determinables and determinates. A determinable is a property described broadly, such as color, shape, or mass. A determinate is a more exact way of having that property, such as red, rectangular, or a particular mass. The relation between them is called determination. It is not quite the same as putting things together with “and,” and it is not quite the same as making a list with “or.” The entry also explains that determination can have several levels, such as color, red, and scarlet. Philosophers have offered different accounts. Some say determinables are not really part of the world; others say they are real but can be explained using determinates; still others say determinables are real and cannot be reduced to them. The topic matters because broad properties appear in scientific laws, explanations of causes, and theories about things that may be genuinely unclear or unfinished.
key_ideas: A determinable is broad, while a determinate is more specific.
Properties can form levels: red is more specific than color but less specific than scarlet.
Different determinates of one kind are often similar in one respect and cannot usually be had together at the same level.
Philosophers disagree about whether determinables are real features of things or only ways we group more specific properties.
These ideas may help explain science, causes, and cases where reality seems not fully settled.
summaries.why_it_matters: We often describe things without giving every possible detail. Understanding how broad and specific properties fit together helps us think carefully about ordinary descriptions and scientific explanations. It also raises a big question: does the world itself contain broad features, or do people add that broadness through language and thought?

important_terms.definition: A broad property that can be made more exact in different ways, such as color, shape, or mass.
A more specific version of a determinable, such as red as a kind of color or oval as a kind of shape.
The relation in which a more specific property gives a particular way of having a broader property.
The idea that one thing can be more exact or detailed than another in a particular respect.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be colored without having one exact color?
Are red and blue similar because they share the property color, or only because we group them together?
Could two different exact shapes belong to one broader kind?
Why might scientists use a broad property instead of listing every tiny detail?

summaries.example: Suppose a scientist describes a particle as having a certain mass without specifying every possible physical detail. “Mass” functions as a determinable, while a precise mass value is a determinate. The precise value entails that the particle has mass, but having mass does not by itself select that one value. This illustrates asymmetric dependence: the more specific property guarantees the broader one, while the reverse does not follow.
summaries.summary: The entry examines determination as a relation of specification among properties and, possibly, other kinds of entities. If red determines color, then being red is being colored in a particular way. Determination is normally non-conjunctive: red is not simply color plus an unrelated additional property. It is also unlike ordinary disjunction, since red and blue are similar as colors and generally incompatible at the same level. Determination can be hierarchical and relative, so red may be a determinate of color and a determinable of scarlet. The entry identifies further proposed features, including inheritance of determinables, asymmetric modal dependence, and causal compatibility between determinates and determinables. It then compares anti-realism, reductionism, and non-reductionism. Reductionists may analyze a determinable as a disjunction or another construction from determinates. Non-reductionists may appeal to essences, causal powers, constitution, or grounding. The philosophical stakes include whether reality is fundamentally maximally specific, how scientific laws express general patterns, how higher-level properties can be causally relevant, and whether indeterminacy can be a feature of reality rather than merely of language or knowledge.
key_ideas: Determination differs from genus-species, conjunction, and disjunction relations.
Determination is normally treated as irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive, forming an ordered pattern of specificity.
The determinable/determinate classification is often relative: red is determinate with respect to color but determinable with respect to scarlet.
Same-level determinates are usually similar and comparable in the relevant respect, while also functioning as exclusive alternatives.
The source surveys anti-realist, reductionist, and non-reductive accounts, none of which is presented as decisively settling the debate.
Applications include scientific laws, higher-level or mental causation, and metaphysical indeterminacy.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction connects ordinary classification with deep questions in metaphysics and philosophy of science. It asks whether generality and incompleteness are merely features of our descriptions or whether they belong to reality itself. The answer affects how we understand laws, explanation, causation, fundamentality, and cases in which no unique most-specific state is available.

important_terms.definition: A property that admits of more specific specifications, such as color, shape, mass, or a relation.
A property that specifies a determinable in a particular way, such as scarlet as a determinate of color through red.
A distinctive, usually non-conjunctive relation of increased specificity between a determinate and its determinable.
The relation in which a determinate entails its determinable, while the determinable can be instantiated without that particular determinate.
The claim that a more specific property is not simply the broader property combined with an independent extra property.
The claim that same-level determinates under one determinable are typically incompatible, such as being uniformly red and blue in the same respect at once.
The view that determinables exist but are metaphysically identical to, or constructed from, determinate properties.
The view that determinables exist and are not metaphysically reducible to constructions from determinates.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a determinate not naturally analyzed as a conjunction of its determinable and an independent property?
Does asymmetric necessitation show that determinates are more fundamental than determinables?
Can a disjunctive analysis explain why determinates within one family resemble one another?
Should exceptions involving sounds, tastes, iridescent objects, or quantum cases weaken the general principles of determination?
Can mental properties be determinables of physical properties without creating causal overdetermination?

summaries.example: Imagine a color chart. “Color” is a broad category, and “red” is one way to specify it. “Scarlet” is a still more exact way to specify red. If a shirt is scarlet, it must be red and colored. But if a shirt is red, it does not have to be scarlet; it might be crimson or burgundy. This one-way pattern is a central feature of determination.
summaries.summary: The entry studies a special relationship between broad and specific properties. Color is a determinable, while red, blue, and other shades are determinates. The relationship can continue through levels: red determines color, while scarlet determines red. This means that the words “determinable” and “determinate” are often relative rather than absolute. Determination also seems different from familiar logical relations. A determinate is not simply a determinable joined with an extra independent feature, and a determinable is not just an ordinary list of alternatives. Same-level determinates are generally similar in the relevant respect and often incompatible, while a determinate always brings along its determinables. The entry describes several historical discussions, including Aristotle’s possible precursor ideas and W. E. Johnson’s systematic treatment. Contemporary philosophers divide over whether determinables are unreal, reducible to determinate properties, or genuine features that cannot be reduced. These options are tested through questions about perception, scientific laws, causal powers, higher-level properties, and metaphysical indeterminacy.
key_ideas: Determination organizes properties by degrees of exactness.
A property can be a determinate in one comparison and a determinable in another.
Determinate properties in the same family are usually alike in one respect, but they may exclude one another at the same level.
Philosophers disagree about whether determinables are genuine features of reality or useful classifications made by language and thought.
Some accounts reduce determinables to determinates, while others treat them as real and irreducible.
The debate has consequences for science, mental causation, and genuine uncertainty in the world.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction helps explain how one description can be both true and less precise than another. It also shows why broad scientific concepts can be useful without listing every detail. More deeply, it asks whether the world contains genuine levels of specification and whether something can be real even when it is not maximally exact.

important_terms.definition: A general property that can have more exact forms, such as color, shape, or mass.
A more exact property that specifies a determinable, such as red as a color or oval as a shape.
The relation between a broader property and a more specific property that gives one particular way of having it.
A property’s degree of exactness relative to another property; scarlet is more specific than red.
The idea that having a determinate guarantees having its determinable, but having the determinable does not guarantee that one determinate.
A relation in which properties are combined, as in being red and square; determination is presented as different from this.
A relation formed by alternatives, as in red or blue; determination is presented as different from an ordinary disjunction.

questions_to_think_about: Is “red” more like a broad category, a real property, or both?
Why is “red or round” not a determinable in the same way that color is?
If two things are different shades of red, what explains their similarity?
Could a broad property be real even if no single exact determinate is selected?
What would happen to scientific explanations if every property had to be described in maximum detail?
